summary: Lisa Orr frames Zapier's challenge as 'app erosion': their 8,000+ integrations built on third-party APIs constantly break as APIs change and deprecate, creating a backlog crisis where support tickets arrive faster than they can be handled. Two parallel experiments were launched. Experiment one empowered support team members to ship code fixes, starting with four target apps and engineering review of merge requests. Experiment two, led by Orr, explored using AI codegen under the project name 'Scout.' Discovery work revealed that the biggest pain point was context gathering—searching API docs, crawling the internet, and reviewing logs—which consumed significant time. Initial tools were built as APIs hosted in a web playground called 'autocode,' but this failed because engineers had to leave their workflows. The Diagnosis API became a 'support darling' and was embedded into their Jira ticket creation process. MCP enabled embedding tools directly into engineers' IDEs via Cursor, but Diagnosis took too long to run synchronously, and adoption of individual tools was scattered. The team hypothesized that orchestrating tools together would deliver more value, leading to Scout Agent. Scout autonomously categorizes issues, assesses fixability, generates merge requests via a GitLab CI/CD pipeline with plan, execute, and validate phases, and attaches results to Jira tickets. Support team members review and request adjustments directly in GitLab via chat, triggering rapid iteration. Scout drives 40% of support's app fixes, increasing per-person velocity from 1-2 to 3-4 tickets per week. Evaluation tracks categorization accuracy, fixability assessment, and solution quality. Orr emphasizes support's three superpowers: proximity to customer pain, real-time troubleshooting with fresh context (including log access that may expire if tickets sit in engineering backlogs), and direct customer relationships ensuring solutions validate against the reporting customer's actual needs. Support team members who participated in the experiment have since become engineers. Orr closes with acknowledgments to the team (including Andy in the audience), a hiring note, and a recommendation to raft the Grand Canyon with ORS.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Grand Canyon Analogy and App Erosion Problem
sections.summary: Orr opens with a Grand Canyon rafting analogy to introduce the concept of 'app erosion'—Zapier's 8,000+ integrations built on third-party APIs that constantly change and break, creating reliability issues, poor customer experience, and churn. A backlog crisis prompted two parallel experiments: empowering support to fix bugs, and exploring AI codegen to accelerate fixes.

sections.title: Experiment One: Support Shipping Code
sections.summary: Experiment one began two years ago to empower support team members to ship code fixes, starting with four target apps and engineering review of merge requests. Support members were eager for engineering experience and many were already unofficially helping maintain apps.

sections.title: Experiment Two: Scout Project Discovery and Initial Tool Building
sections.summary: Discovery work through dog fooding and shadowing revealed context gathering as the biggest pain point. Initial APIs were built including Diagnosis (LLM-powered context curation) and a test case finder. A web playground called 'autocode' was created but failed to get engagement because it was 'one more window to go to.' Cursor's launch made some tools redundant. However, Diagnosis became a 'support darling' and was embedded into their Jira ticket creation process via a Zapier integration.

sections.title: MCP Tools and Adoption Challenges
sections.summary: MCP enabled embedding tools into engineers' Cursor workflows, reducing IDE departures. However, Diagnosis was too slow for synchronous use, customization needs weren't met (engineers turned to Zapier's own MCP), and adoption was scattered across the tool suite. The team hypothesized that orchestrating tools together would deliver more value than individual usage.

sections.title: Scout Agent: Orchestration and Workflow
sections.summary: Scout Agent was created to orchestrate tools autonomously. It categorizes issues, assesses fixability, generates merge requests via a GitLab CI/CD pipeline (plan, execute, validate phases) using Scout MCP tools and Cursor SDK, and attaches results to Jira. Support reviews and can request adjustments directly in GitLab via chat, triggering rapid iteration. The support team became the first customer due to high-volume, low-complexity tickets.

sections.title: Impact and Support Team Superpowers
sections.summary: Scout drives 40% of support's app fixes, increasing per-person velocity from 1-2 to 3-4 tickets per week. Evaluation tracks categorization, fixability, and solution quality at 75% accuracy for the first two. Engineering benefits by focusing on complex work. Orr identifies support's three superpowers: proximity to customer pain, real-time troubleshooting with fresh context, and direct customer relationships.

sections.title: Support Validation Advantage and Closing
sections.summary: Orr elaborates on support's validation superpower: engineers working from a backlog months later may lose log access and produce solutions that change behavior without fitting the specific reporting customer's needs. Support team members who participated in the experiment have since become engineers. She closes with acknowledgments to the team (including Andy in the audience), a hiring note, and a recommendation to raft the Grand Canyon with ORS.
